questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which investigation is first line for suspected gallstones, and what is its main limitation?
options: Ultrasonography, which is insensitive for stones in the common bile duct
Computed tomography, which misses gallbladder stones
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, which is unavailable
Plain radiography, which shows most stones
questions.concept: Only about 10 to 15 percent of gallstones are radio-opaque, and a dilated duct with deranged liver tests prompts magnetic resonance cholangiography or endoscopic ultrasound.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which clinical picture distinguishes acute cholecystitis from biliary colic?
options: Persistent right upper quadrant pain beyond a few hours with fever, leucocytosis and Murphy sign
Pain radiating to the back with vomiting
questions.concept: Biliary colic results from transient cystic duct obstruction without inflammation, whereas persistent obstruction produces inflammation and, if untreated, empyema, gangrene or perforation.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which triad describes acute cholangitis, and what is the priority of treatment?
options: Charcot triad of fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain, treated by antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage
questions.concept: Addition of hypotension and confusion gives the Reynolds pentad of suppurative cholangitis, which mandates emergency decompression by endoscopic retrograde cholangiography.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding indicates that cholecystectomy should be performed during the index admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis?
options: Resolution of the pancreatitis, because delay carries a high risk of recurrent biliary events
questions.concept: Trials show fewer readmissions with same-admission surgery in mild disease, whereas in severe pancreatitis with collections surgery is deferred for several weeks.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which score or marker is used to predict severity in acute pancreatitis within the first 48 hours?
options: Modified Glasgow or APACHE II score with C-reactive protein above 150 mg per litre at 48 hours
questions.concept: Enzyme levels correlate with diagnosis rather than severity, whereas persistent organ failure beyond 48 hours defines severe disease under the revised Atlanta classification.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which complication of acute pancreatitis presents at 4 weeks or later with a persistent mass and early satiety?
options: A pseudocyst, a collection with a defined wall and no solid debris
questions.concept: Intervention is reserved for symptoms, infection or obstruction rather than size alone, and endoscopic transgastric drainage has largely replaced open surgery.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why does Courvoisier's law state that a palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice is unlikely to be due to stones?
options: Chronic inflammation from stones makes the gallbladder fibrotic and unable to distend, so painless distension suggests malignant distal obstruction
questions.concept: Exceptions include a stone impacted in the cystic duct with a mucocele and double pathology, which is why it is a guide rather than a rule.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why is the critical view of safety sought during laparoscopic cholecystectomy?
options: Demonstrating two and only two structures entering the gallbladder within a cleared hepatocystic triangle prevents misidentification of the common bile duct
It confirms the absence of stones
It identifies the cystic artery only
questions.concept: Bile duct injury is the most serious complication and usually results from misidentification rather than from technical failure, which is why this anatomical checkpoint is emphasised.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Gallbladder and Bile Ducts

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which lesion classically presents with a lucid interval after a blow to the temple, and what is its source?
options: Extradural haematoma from the middle meningeal artery
Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a berry aneurysm
questions.concept: The convex biconvex collection limited by suture lines on computed tomography is characteristic, and prompt evacuation gives an excellent outcome because the underlying brain is often undamaged.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Neurosurgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which appearance on computed tomography indicates a chronic subdural haematoma?
options: A crescentic hypodense collection crossing suture lines
questions.concept: It is commonest in the elderly and in alcohol users after trivial trauma, presents with fluctuating confusion or headache, and is drained through burr holes.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Neurosurgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which measure lowers intracranial pressure most rapidly in a deteriorating head-injured patient?
options: Head elevation with hyperosmolar therapy such as mannitol or hypertonic saline
Prophylactic hyperventilation to a carbon dioxide of 25 mmHg
questions.concept: Corticosteroids increase mortality in head injury as shown in CRASH, and prolonged aggressive hyperventilation causes ischaemic vasoconstriction, so both are avoided.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Neurosurgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which cerebral perfusion pressure is generally targeted in severe traumatic brain injury, and how is it calculated?
options: About 60 to 70 mmHg, calculated as mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure
Equal to the mean arterial pressure
questions.concept: Because both hypotension and raised intracranial pressure reduce perfusion, avoiding a single episode of hypotension is as important as controlling pressure.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Neurosurgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which finding on examination indicates uncal herniation and imminent brainstem compression?
options: An ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil with contralateral hemiparesis and deteriorating consciousness
questions.concept: The oculomotor nerve is compressed against the tentorial edge, and Kernohan notch phenomenon can produce ipsilateral weakness, which is a well-recognised false localising sign.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Neurosurgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why is diffuse axonal injury associated with poor outcome despite a normal initial computed tomogram?
options: Shearing of axons at grey-white junctions and the corpus callosum is not visible on early computed tomography but causes widespread functional disconnection
It always shows on the first scan
questions.concept: Magnetic resonance imaging with gradient echo and diffusion sequences demonstrates it, and the mismatch between imaging and the depth of coma is the classic clue.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Neurosurgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which vaccination is required before elective splenectomy, and how long in advance?
options: Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccines, ideally 2 weeks before surgery
Hepatitis B alone, on the day of surgery
questions.concept: Lifelong penicillin prophylaxis in children and in the first years after surgery, together with patient education and an emergency antibiotic supply, complete the protection against overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Liver and Spleen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which imaging finding suggests an amoebic rather than a pyogenic liver abscess?
options: A single lesion in the right lobe in a patient with a travel or dysentery history, with positive amoebic serology
questions.concept: Amoebic abscess responds to metronidazole with a luminal agent and rarely needs drainage, whereas pyogenic abscess needs drainage and treatment of the biliary or portal source.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Liver and Spleen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which cystic liver lesion must not be aspirated without precautions, and why?
options: Hydatid cyst, because spillage risks anaphylaxis and dissemination
questions.concept: The PAIR technique with albendazole cover, or surgery with careful field protection, is used, and the Casoni test is obsolete with serology and imaging making the diagnosis.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Liver and Spleen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which operation decompresses portal hypertension while preserving hepatic portal perfusion?
questions.concept: Non-selective shunts decompress effectively but divert portal flow away from the liver, increasing encephalopathy, which is why selective shunts and transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt have largely replaced them.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Liver and Spleen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which measure is first line for acute variceal bleeding after resuscitation?
options: Endoscopic band ligation with a vasoactive drug such as terlipressin and antibiotic prophylaxis
questions.concept: Antibiotics reduce mortality independently by preventing bacterial infection, and balloon tamponade is only a bridge for up to 24 hours to definitive treatment.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Liver and Spleen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why does splenic injury in a haemodynamically stable patient increasingly not require splenectomy?
options: Non-operative management with observation, and angioembolisation where needed, preserves immune function with good success rates
questions.concept: Splenic preservation avoids lifelong infection risk, and failure of non-operative management is signalled by haemodynamic instability rather than by the imaging grade alone.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Liver and Spleen

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which investigation is the gold standard for diagnosing achalasia?
options: High-resolution oesophageal manometry showing failed relaxation of the lower sphincter with absent peristalsis
questions.concept: Barium shows the bird-beak narrowing with a dilated body and endoscopy excludes pseudoachalasia from tumour, but the functional diagnosis and subtype require manometry.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Oesophagus and Stomach

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which premalignant condition follows chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux, and what does it predispose to?
options: Barrett oesophagus with intestinal metaplasia, predisposing to adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus
Squamous metaplasia, predisposing to squamous carcinoma
questions.concept: Squamous carcinoma is instead linked to smoking, alcohol, achalasia, corrosive stricture and Plummer-Vinson syndrome, and it dominates the upper two thirds of the oesophagus.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Oesophagus and Stomach

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which sign indicates that a gastric carcinoma has spread to the left supraclavicular node?
questions.concept: Each of these eponymous findings indicates incurable disease, with the umbilical nodule, the rectal shelf on digital examination and the bilateral ovarian deposits representing other routes of spread.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Oesophagus and Stomach

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which operation is appropriate for a carcinoma of the antrum of the stomach, and what lymphadenectomy is standard?
options: Subtotal gastrectomy with a D2 lymphadenectomy
Wedge resection with no nodal clearance
questions.concept: D2 dissection improves staging and, in experienced hands, survival, and a proximal or diffuse tumour requires total gastrectomy to obtain an adequate margin.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Oesophagus and Stomach

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Which complication of gastrectomy presents with sweating, palpitations and diarrhoea within 30 minutes of a meal?
options: Early dumping syndrome from rapid delivery of hyperosmolar chyme into the small bowel
questions.concept: Late dumping occurs 2 to 3 hours after eating from an exaggerated insulin response, and both are managed with small dry meals low in refined carbohydrate.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Oesophagus and Stomach

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.stem: Why is a Helicobacter pylori eradication regimen offered to a patient with gastric MALT lymphoma?
options: Early-stage disease frequently regresses completely after eradication because the lymphoma is antigen driven
It prevents transformation to carcinoma only
It has no effect on the lymphoma
questions.concept: The t(11;18) translocation predicts failure to respond, so those cases proceed to chemotherapy or radiotherapy rather than relying on antibiotics.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Oesophagus and Stomach

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Paediatric surgery: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, hypospadias
questions.stem: Which metabolic abnormality must be corrected before pyloromyotomy, and why?
options: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, because it causes postoperative apnoea if uncorrected
questions.concept: Alkalosis blunts the central respiratory drive, so correction with saline and potassium over 24 to 48 hours is a prerequisite rather than a delay.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Paediatric Surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Paediatric surgery: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, hypospadias
questions.stem: Which imaging confirms hypertrophic pyloric stenosis?
options: Ultrasonography showing a pyloric muscle thickness above 3 mm and channel length above 15 mm
Plain radiograph showing a double bubble
questions.concept: Ultrasound has replaced contrast studies because it is quick, non-irradiating and directly measures the muscle, and the string sign on contrast is now of historical interest.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Paediatric Surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Paediatric surgery: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, hypospadias
questions.stem: Which principle governs the timing of hypospadias repair?
options: Repair at about 6 to 18 months, before body image awareness and after the penis has grown sufficiently
Repair only if there is obstruction
questions.concept: Circumcision must be avoided beforehand because the foreskin is used in reconstruction, and associated chordee and cryptorchidism are addressed at the same time.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Paediatric Surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Paediatric surgery: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, hypospadias
questions.stem: Which age and lead point pattern distinguishes idiopathic from pathological intussusception?
options: Idiopathic disease peaks at 6 to 18 months from hypertrophied Peyer patches, whereas beyond 2 years a lead point such as a polyp, Meckel diverticulum or lymphoma is likely
Pathological cases are commoner in infants
questions.concept: Finding a lead point changes management because reduction alone will be followed by recurrence, so resection of the causative lesion is needed.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Paediatric Surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Paediatric surgery: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, hypospadias
questions.stem: Which finding contraindicates air enema reduction of intussusception?
questions.concept: Successful reduction is confirmed by free reflux of air into the small bowel, and recurrence occurs in about 10 percent, most within 72 hours.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Paediatric Surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Paediatric surgery: intussusception, pyloric stenosis, hypospadias
questions.stem: Why is an undescended testis brought down before the age of about 1 year?
options: Germ cell degeneration begins in the first year and early orchidopexy improves fertility and allows surveillance for malignancy
questions.concept: Orchidopexy does not abolish the increased cancer risk but makes the testis examinable, and a non-palpable testis requires laparoscopic assessment.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. Paediatric Surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Salivary glands, neck swellings & oral cavity carcinoma
questions.stem: Which is the commonest salivary gland tumour, and what is the risk of enucleation rather than formal excision?
options: Pleomorphic adenoma, which recurs because of pseudopodia extending beyond an incomplete capsule
questions.concept: Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation is the standard operation, and long-standing tumours carry a small risk of carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Salivary Glands and Neck

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Salivary glands, neck swellings & oral cavity carcinoma
questions.stem: Which malignant salivary tumour is notorious for perineural spread and late distant metastasis?
questions.concept: Its indolent but relentless course means recurrence and pulmonary metastasis may appear a decade later, so long-term follow-up and attention to nerve margins are required.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Salivary Glands and Neck

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Salivary glands, neck swellings & oral cavity carcinoma
questions.stem: Which neck swelling moves upward on protrusion of the tongue, and which operation prevents recurrence?
options: Thyroglossal cyst, treated by the Sistrunk operation removing the tract and the central hyoid
Branchial cyst, treated by simple excision
questions.concept: Because the tract passes behind the body of the hyoid to the foramen caecum, simple excision leaves it behind and recurrence follows.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Salivary Glands and Neck

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Salivary glands, neck swellings & oral cavity carcinoma
questions.stem: Which nerve is at greatest risk during excision of the submandibular gland, and what is the deficit?
options: The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve, causing drooping of the corner of the mouth
The hypoglossal nerve, causing tongue deviation
The lingual nerve, causing loss of taste
questions.concept: The lingual and hypoglossal nerves are also at risk deep in the field, so the incision is placed at least two finger-breadths below the mandible to protect the marginal branch.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Salivary Glands and Neck

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Salivary glands, neck swellings & oral cavity carcinoma
questions.stem: Which factor most influences the management of a squamous carcinoma of the oral cavity with a clinically negative neck?
options: Depth of invasion, since beyond about 4 mm elective neck dissection is indicated because of occult nodal disease
questions.concept: The randomised evidence favouring elective over therapeutic neck dissection for depth-positive tumours changed practice, and depth is now part of the staging system.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Salivary Glands and Neck

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.topic: Salivary glands, neck swellings & oral cavity carcinoma
questions.stem: Why does a persistent lateral neck lump with cystic squamous cells on aspiration in an adult require investigation of the oropharynx?
options: It is more likely a cystic metastasis from a human papillomavirus-associated tonsillar or base of tongue carcinoma than a branchial cyst
Branchial cysts are commonest in adults
questions.concept: Excising it as a benign cyst delays diagnosis and compromises later treatment, so panendoscopy with tonsillectomy and imaging is undertaken to find the primary.
questions.reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 27e, Ch. The Salivary Glands and Neck
